summary: Defines a YANG module that lets a NETCONF client get notifications about common events on a server, such as a change in its capabilities. Management applications often need to know about such events.

eli5.summary: A network manager wants a ping when something changes on a device. This defines the standard alerts a device can send, like "my abilities changed".

subtitle: A YANG module that lets a NETCONF client hear about config, capability and session events.

tldr.problem: Management applications need to know about common events on a NETCONF server, such as a change in its capabilities, but there was no standard way to get them.
tldr.mechanism: A YANG module defines five notifications for the NETCONF stream: config change, capability change, session start, session end and confirmed commit. Clients get them through the subscription mechanism of RFC 5277.
tldr.outcome: Servers report these base events in a standard form. The notifications can reveal sensitive details, so read access has to be controlled.

today: RFC 6470 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Base Notifications
sections.content:
The NETCONF protocol (RFC 6241) provides mechanisms to manipulate configuration datastores. Client applications also often need to be aware of common events, such as a change in server capabilities, that may affect management applications.

RFC 6470 responds with a YANG module (RFC 6020) that lets a NETCONF client receive notifications for some common system events. Terms such as client, server, datastore, event, stream and subscription come from RFC 6241, RFC 5277 and RFC 6020.
sections.eli5: Managers of network devices want to be told when something important changes. This document makes a standard way to tell them.

sections.title: Module Overview
sections.content:
The module defines a small number of event notifications for the NETCONF stream, reachable through the subscription mechanism in RFC 5277. It imports types from the ietf-netconf module (RFC 6241) and ietf-inet-types (RFC 6021).

The notifications pertain to configuration and monitoring parts of the managed system, not the entire system. A server MUST report events directly related to the NETCONF protocol. It MAY report events for non-NETCONF management sessions, using the session-id value of zero.
sections.eli5: Anyone can sign up to a channel called NETCONF to receive these alerts. The device must report NETCONF happenings and may also report other ways people manage it.

sections.title: The Five Notifications
sections.content:
The module defines these notifications:

  • netconf-config-change: the <running> or <startup> datastore was changed by a management session. It summarizes the edits detected.
  • netconf-capability-change: server capabilities changed, listing which were added, deleted or modified.
  • netconf-session-start: a session started, with the identity of the user.
  • netconf-session-end: a session ended, with the user and the reason it ended.
  • netconf-confirmed-commit: a confirmed-commit event occurred, with the current state of the procedure.

How a capability is changed is outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: There are five kinds of alert: settings changed, abilities changed, someone arrived, someone left, and a try-it-and-confirm change moved forward.

sections.title: Shared Fields and Config Changes
sections.content:
Two groupings are reused. common-session-parms holds a mandatory username, a mandatory session-id and an optional source-host IP address. A NETCONF session MUST be identified by a non-zero session id, while a non-NETCONF session MAY use zero.

changed-by-parms holds a changed-by container. If the server itself caused the change, the empty leaf server is present. Otherwise the name, remote host and session ID of the responsible session are reported.

A config-change notification adds a datastore leaf, either running (the default) or startup, and a list of edit records with a target node and the operation performed. The server SHOULD include an edit record for each distinct edit it detected, and MAY omit the list if the details are unknown. It MAY also generate the notification while loading a datastore during boot.
sections.eli5: Every alert says who did it, from where, and what changed, a bit like a security camera log.

sections.title: Capabilities, Sessions and Confirmed Commits
sections.content:
A capability-change notification has the added-capability, deleted-capability and modified-capability lists of URIs. A capability counts as modified when its base URI is unchanged but the parameters at the end of the URI changed, and the full new URI is returned.

A session-end notification includes a mandatory termination-reason: closed, killed, dropped, timeout, bad-hello or other. When the reason is killed, the killed-by leaf gives the session that caused it, if known.

A confirmed-commit notification has a mandatory confirm-event: start, cancel, timeout, extend or complete. For start and extend a timeout leaf in seconds gives the approximate time until the timeout might occur. For the timeout event, the session parameters are not present.
sections.eli5: When someone leaves, the alert says why, such as they logged out, got kicked off, lost the connection or sat idle too long.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is accessed through NETCONF, whose lowest layer is a secure transport. The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH (RFC 6242).

Some readable nodes may be sensitive, so read access via get, get-config or notification needs to be controlled. The RFC walks through each notification. Config-change events can alert an attacker that specific data was altered, and the edit data could show whether vulnerabilities may now be present. Capability changes could help an attacker identify a device, for example by learning that a packet capture capability was added. Session events show when another session may be editing an unlocked datastore. A confirmed-commit event can signal that the device behavior has changed.
sections.eli5: These alerts tell a story about what a device is doing, so only trusted people should be allowed to see them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document registers one XML namespace URN, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-netconf-notifications, in the IETF XML registry (RFC 3688). It also registers one module in the YANG Module Names registry, named ietf-netconf-notifications with the prefix ncn.
sections.eli5: The module is put in the official lists so nobody else uses the same name.

items.label: closed
items.desc: Client ended the session normally, for example with close-session.

items.label: killed
items.desc: Ended abnormally, for example by kill-session.

items.label: timeout
items.desc: Inactive, for example waiting for hello or rpc messages.

items.label: bad-hello
items.desc: The client's hello message was invalid.
